summary:
Saudi Arabia is among the most dangerous jurisdictions for a transgender person who is identified. The kingdom has no codified penal code. Judges apply an uncodified interpretation of sharia drawn from the Quran and the Sunnah, so penalties for same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity are unpredictable and range from fines and flogging through lengthy or indeterminate imprisonment to death in the most severe cases.

Deviation from traditional gender norms is itself treated as a criminal offence, not merely incidental conduct attached to another charge. In October 2021, five Saudi men were arrested in the Northern Borders province after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage on social media, showing that cross-dressing enforcement is active and reaches online expression as well as conduct in public.

No legal gender recognition is available, same-sex relationships carry no legal status, and no discrimination protections exist. LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in the country, so there is no formal protection machinery a trans visitor could turn to.

Enforcement has proved lethal. Mohammad Amin, a Pakistani transgender woman known as Meeno, died in Saudi custody after a roundup with 34 others at Azizia prison in Riyadh. Activists from her home country reported that she was beaten with clubs and hosepipes, aggravating a chronic heart condition; Saudi authorities attributed the death to a heart attack, and her family and trans-rights activists dispute the official account.

Prosecution reaches travellers for expression published before they enter the country. Amnesty International documented a business analyst arrested at Riyadh airport on 31 August 2024 as he was returning to the UK with his family, targeted for social media posts written before his arrival.

Entry and exit visa paperwork does not ask about sexual orientation, but it does record nationality, sex, religion and marital status. Work-visa applicants must pass an HIV test on arrival and before permit renewal, and foreign applicants found to be infected are deported; deportation is also available as a penalty for homosexuality itself. Since tourist visas were introduced in 2019, a Public Decency Law has fined public displays of affection and immodest clothing, giving enforcement officers a further basis for action against gender-nonconforming visitors.

Official assurances of welcome carry no legal effect. A May 2023 update to the Saudi Tourism Authority's FAQ page stated that all visitors, including LGBTQ visitors, are welcome, and VisitSaudi states that privacy will be respected, while homosexuality remains illegal and enforcement continues. The UK government advises that legal action is uncommon but recommends that couples avoid public affection, and warns that trans travellers could face difficulties with dress codes and access to medical care because trans status is not recognised.

Access to care is unreliable. The government has designated several hospitals to treat people with AIDS and HIV, but other hospitals often refuse care or treat patients without compassion, and condoms were until recently rarely available outside certain hospitals and medical supply stores.

A closed 2005 trial in Jeddah of dozens of Saudi men arrested at a party described as a gay wedding produced sentences totalling 14,200 lashes and up to two years in prison, handed down without defence lawyers. A Human Rights Watch researcher described prosecuting and imprisoning people for homosexual conduct as flagrant human rights violations, and the case shows the severity Saudi courts have imposed.

Official hostility is expressed outside the courts as well. In June 2022, officials in Riyadh seized rainbow-coloured products in a crackdown framed as curbing the promotion of homosexuality. In September 2013, Gulf states discussed a proposal to test and ban gay foreigners, which officials later downplayed as a mere proposal.
tangentialFactors:
A3M Global Monitoring's LGBTQ+ Risk Map for 2024/25 places Saudi Arabia among the least safe destinations for LGBTQ travellers, in a ranking that also lists Somalia, Yemen, Uganda, Afghanistan, the UAE, Tanzania, Malaysia and Pakistan.

Bars and nightclubs are illegal. Public movie theatres, permitted only since 2018, have LGBTQ themes edited out of films, and customs maintains a banned list of films and television shows, so no venues of the kind a trans visitor might use exist in legal form.

Observers reported that MDLBeast Soundstorm, an annual multi-day music festival in Riyadh, included public display of LGBTQI+ culture, while appearing to support homosexuality can result in prosecution for individuals and clubs alike. Open expression at such events therefore sits against an unchanged legal backdrop.
localsOnly:
Public education is required to teach Islamic values that strongly condemn homosexuality. Ministry of Education textbooks described homosexuality as one of the most disgusting sins and greatest crimes and specified capital punishment for public homosexual intercourse, though the ministry was found in 2020 to have removed the death-penalty condemnation from textbooks.

In 2012, the government asked the Committee for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice to help expel students judged to be gay or lesbian on the basis of their mannerisms and fashion taste, applying gender presentation as a basis for exclusion from schooling.

HIV prevention education for men who have sex with men is minimal. A 2024 report by the national AIDS programme makes some mention of them, and condoms were until recently rarely available outside certain hospitals and medical supply stores.

The June 2022 seizure of rainbow-coloured goods explicitly targeted the young generation, confiscating children's hair accessories, backpacks, pencil cases and rainbow-striped crayon packs.

Private schools, which mainly serve expatriate families, have discretion over their curriculum on homosexuality.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory establishes how Saudi authorities handle a change of sex marker on a passport or national identity document, or whether border officers screen travellers on gender presentation. This remains unresolved rather than absent.

The inventory documents individual enforcement cases and historical sentences but supplies no sentencing statistics for gender-nonconformity charges, so the frequency of prosecution relative to the severity of penalties cannot be stated.

Whether the May 2023 tourism-authority welcome statement has any operational effect on visa issuance or border decisions is not sourced, and the status of the 2013 proposal to test and ban gay foreigners remains, as officials described it, a proposal that was never confirmed as policy.
